Tonga ratifies U.N. Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
item.description: Tonga has ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Tonga's UN Ambassador, H.E. Mr. Viliami Vaʻinga Tōnē, deposited the instrument of ratification with the United Nations on 4 September.
item.content:encoded:
Tonga has ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

Tonga's UN Ambassador, H.E. Mr. Viliami Vaʻinga Tōnē, deposited the instrument of ratification with the United Nations on 4 September.

He said it was a milestone in Tonga’s commitment to advancing the rights and dignity of persons with disabilities.

The Instrument of Ratification was signed by King Tupou VI on 21 August 2026, following the completion of Tonga’s national processes.

Ambassador Tōnē stated, “It was deposited together with an accompanying declaration and reservations reflecting Tonga’s unique and special circumstances as a small island developing State, the needs of its people and relevant provisions of its domestic laws.”

“The ratification represents an important step forward for Tonga and reflects the Kingdom’s determination to promote a more inclusive society in which persons with disabilities can participate fully and equally, while recognising the country’s particular national circumstances and the need for implementation that is both effective and responsive to the realities of its people.”

He stated that the treaty action also carries wider significance for Tonga’s enduring commitment to multilateralism, international cooperation and the rules-based international system.

It reinforces the inclusion and sustainable development pillars of the United Nations agenda and advances the central pledge of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development to leave no one behind.

item.title: Pacific heads call out Australia on fossil fuel exports
item.description: Of all the testimonies about the impact of global warming heard at the Pacific Islands Forum summit, Maina Talia's may be the most heart-wrenching. The Tuvalu climate change minister has been a relentless ambassador for lifting climate ambition, given the imminent threat to his homeland.
item.content:encoded:
Of all the testimonies about the impact of global warming heard at the Pacific Islands Forum summit, Maina Talia's may be the most heart-wrenching.

The Tuvalu climate change minister has been a relentless ambassador for lifting climate ambition, given the imminent threat to his homeland.

He was distraught as he recalled reading the UN Environment Programme's grim assessment of warming trajectories, released on Wednesday.

" I couldn't sleep last night thinking, 'how are we going to prepare ourselves'," he said in Palau.

" Because the scenarios that may happen in the next 100 years or so, could happen within the next 10 years or so.

" It's real now. It's here now. It's no longer a distant threat for the Pacific, and it's a call for all of us to scale climate actions."

The dispiriting findings in the UNEP report include a best-case scenario of a 1.8 degree temperature rise above pre-industrial levels.

That is past a scientifically-backed tipping point, when temperature rises become much harder to stop because of flow-on effects.

With a highest point of just under five metres above sea level, for Tuvalu and Mr Talia, there can be no navigating the climate with warming over 1.5 per cent.

The UNEP report states "the policy challenge has shifted from avoiding overshoot to navigating it".

The risks, at even the UNEP 's best case scenario, include ice sheet collapse, deforestation and the thawing of permafrost: outcomes which would trigger further warming and/or sea level rise.

" The 1.5 has been central to the discussion ... for the past many years, and we will continue to push for that," Mr Talia said.

" The only way out for us is to ensure that we continue to push for 1.5 to stay alive, to stay in our countries."

It was five years ago, in an address to the COP26 climate talks, that Mr Talia's predecessor Simon Kofe won the world's attention for a video address while standing in thigh-deep water.

Since then, Tuvalu and Australia have signed the Falepili, a groundbreaking pact with a security element and climate adaptation, but also a resettlement ballot for Tuvalu citizens.

Some, like Mr Talia, do not intend to take up that option.

Alongside Mr Talia in Palau was Ralph Regenvanu, the Vanuatu climate change minister who led a successful case to the International Court of Justice finding high-emitting countries have a legal duty to stop climate harm.

" Australia is not doing enough. Australia is a major producer of fossil fuels. We all know fossil fuels are the primary driver of the climate crisis," Mr Regenvanu said.

" The very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that.

" This means a rapid transitioning away from fossil fuels and fossil fuel subsidies. There's no other way."

The Climate Council states the Albanese Government had approved 36 new, expanded or extended coal, oil and gas projects to March 2026.

In Palau, Mr Albanese defended his government's record, saying the grid had recently hit 50 per cent supply from renewables, and Pacific leaders understood a transition would take time.

" Australia is highly regarded when it comes to climate change ... Pacific leaders have respect for the position that we've taken," he said.

Australia is also a big supporter of the Pacific's push to become a 100 per cent renewable region, as championed by Palau President Surangel Whipps.

On Thursday, Mr Albanese and Mr Whipps will visit an Australia-backed solar panel farm which will bump Palau's share of renewable-powered electricity generation to 25 per cent.

" Palau has shown strong leadership on climate action and sustainable development, and Australia is proud to support those efforts," Mr Albanese said.

item.title: Fanongonongo - Kau Kanititeiti kuo lesisita ki he fili-si'i
item.description: FANONGONONGO - KAU KANITITEITI KUO LESISITA KI HE FILI - SIÍ KI HE FAKAFOFONGA FALEALEA KI TONGATAPU 2 & ONGO NIUA 17 Óku ou fakaápaápa mo fanongonongo atu heni á kinautolu kuo lava á hono lesisita ko e kau Kanititeiti ki he Fili-si'i ki he Fakafofonga ó e Kakai ki Falealea maáe Vahenga Fili Tongatapu 2 mo e Ongo Niua 17, á ia naé tapuni í he áho ni Tuápulelulu 3 ó Sepitema, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
FANONGONONGO - KAU KANITITEITI KUO LESISITA KI HE FILI - SIÍ KI HE FAKAFOFONGA FALEALEA KI TONGATAPU 2 & ONGO NIUA 17

Óku ou fakaápaápa mo fanongonongo atu heni á kinautolu kuo lava á hono lesisita ko e kau Kanititeiti ki he Fili-si'i ki he Fakafofonga ó e Kakai ki Falealea maáe Vahenga Fili Tongatapu 2 mo e Ongo Niua 17, á ia naé tapuni í he áho ni Tuápulelulu 3 ó Sepitema, 2026.

Naé fakahoko ai pe mo hono toho ó honau fika takitaha ki he hokohoko ó e Pepa Paloti, á ia óku anga pehe ni:

Fakatokangaí ange ko e lesisita fili ki he Fili-sií ni é tapuni ia í he áho 23 ó Sepitema.

Fakamanatu atu ai pe á e áho ki he Fili-sií ko e áho Tuápulelulu ko hono 8 ó Ókatopa 2026, mei he taimi 9:00 pongipongi ki he 4:00 efiafi.

Ki ha toe fakaikiiki fekauáki mo e fanongonongo ni, kataki ka e fet'utaki mai ki homau 'ulu'i 'ofisi i Ma'ufanga ki he fika 28820.
